description: HSTU - The Golden Flag is five students from Hajee Mohammad Danesh Science and Technology University, Bangladesh. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we are developing Bish-Pani Radar to combine satellite radar and groundwater data for arsenic field-testing triage in the Bengal Delta. Our work spans Earth observation, hydrology, and software. We distinguish measured from demonstration data and communicate uncertainty: ground motion is an indirect indicator, not a measure of water chemistry.
summary: Bish-Pani Radar is a satellite-guided early-warning and field-testing triage tool for groundwater arsenic risk in Bangladesh’s Bengal Delta. It combines verified BGS/DPHE well chemistry and aquifer depths with Sentinel-1 InSAR ground-motion measurements to identify areas where deep aquifers may be under pressure from clay compaction. A Dynamic Aquifer Vulnerability Index prioritizes deep community wells for scarce on-site water testing. The system treats radar as a mechanical proxy for deformation, never as a direct detector of arsenic, and separates measured observations from clearly labeled demonstration data. Its aim is to help health and water teams direct testing sooner while communicating uncertainty and scientific limitations. The current case study also reports a negative radar finding at Site M rather than forcing a hotspot. Developed for Bangladesh, the platform presents mapped risk, well information, and triage guidance.
details:
Bish-Pani Radar combines groundwater observations with satellite radar interferometry to guide field testing. The pipeline ingests 152 verified BGS/DPHE National Hydrochemical Survey boreholes, including well depths and laboratory arsenic/iron measurements, plus the Site M case study from Mihajlov et al. (2020). Real Sentinel-1 track 114/frame 71 interferograms processed through ASF HyP3 are coherence-filtered (γ ≥ 0.35), stacked, corrected for a broad regional ramp, and summarized onto 250 m cells. The web interface maps wells and radar-derived indicators and supports local triage.

The Dynamic Aquifer Vulnerability Index combines static aquifer context, subsidence and seasonal pumping indicators. It distinguishes shallow Holocene wells, where baseline chemistry dominates, from deeper Pleistocene wells, where compaction is a more relevant warning signal. Demonstration wells are labeled separately from measured records.

The method has four safeguards: depth stratification; a SAR coherence quality threshold; exclusion of active river channels; and aggregation to a common grid rather than assigning a radar pixel directly to a point well. In the Site M example, the corrected local rate is −3.4 mm/year and the well is not flagged. This negative result illustrates that arsenic mobilization can occur without a local sinking hotspot.

The intended benefit is to prioritize scarce field test kits and communicate where follow-up sampling may be most useful. DAVI is a screening aid, not an arsenic sensor, a diagnosis, or a substitute for laboratory or field-kit water testing. The system uses Python for processing and a React/TypeScript web interface with Leaflet mapping. NASA/JPL NISAR and ASF resources inform the SAR context; the processed measurements currently described here are Sentinel-1 data, not NISAR observations.
